opus-5.5.text:
I think large language models are an incredibly important milestone, but I don't believe they're the endpoint. Language is a very compressed representation of the world. It's what humans invented to communicate what we already understand, so when you train on text you're inheriting an enormous amount of human knowledge, which is why LLMs feel so smart so quickly. But that's also a limitation. A lot of intelligence never gets written down: how objects move, how you navigate a room, physical intuition, the kind of understanding a baby or an animal has before it ever learns a word.

So my view is that the next phase is going to be much more about grounding: learning from vision, from video, from interaction with the physical world. You could call it world models or spatial intelligence. The goal is a system that doesn't just predict the next token but actually builds an internal model of how the world works and can reason and plan with it.

I also think the current paradigm of scaling up text is starting to hit some walls. High-quality text data is finite, and we're seeing diminishing returns from simply making models bigger. That doesn't mean LLMs will go away. I think they'll become one component, almost like the interface or the reasoning layer, inside a larger system that perceives and acts.

For people working in computer vision, this is actually a very exciting time. For a while vision felt like it was being absorbed into the language paradigm, with images treated as just another kind of token. But I think the community is realizing that visual representation learning has its own fundamental problems that language can't solve for us. If we want truly general intelligence, we have to take seeing and understanding the physical world seriously, not as an add-on to language but as a foundation in its own right.

r001.rationale: The candidate says, “LLMs will not go away,” and predicts they will remain a component of larger systems.

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts LLMs will no longer be the endpoint and will become one component within larger systems, indicating reduced prominence over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I should say up front that I'm not primarily a language model person—most of my work has been on the visual side, on representation learning and generative models. So I see LLMs a bit from the outside, and that shapes how I think about where they're going.

The first thing I'd say is that the scaling story has been remarkable, but I think we're entering a phase where the question is less "how big" and more "what's missing." If you look at what language models are actually good at, it's almost entirely things that are already well-encoded in text. Text is a very compressed, very human-filtered view of the world. It's full of things people bothered to write down. And a huge amount of what makes intelligence useful never gets written down—how objects move, how space works, what happens when you push on something, what a room looks like from a different angle. Humans learn most of that before they can read. Language models are learning the summary without the underlying experience.

So I think the future of large language models is, honestly, that they stop being purely language models. The interesting direction is grounding—connecting these systems to perception, to video, to interaction with an environment. And I'd push back a little on how this is usually done today. The common recipe is to take a vision encoder, bolt it onto a language model, and let the language model do all the thinking. That gives you a system that can describe an image very fluently, but if you probe it on really basic visual things—counting, spatial relationships, whether two objects are the same—it's surprisingly weak. The language prior is doing a lot of the work and sometimes it just hallucinates what "should" be there. I think that tells you the visual representation is still the bottleneck, not the language side.

The second thing I'd say is that I'm quite interested in what the right form of self-supervision looks like in this next phase. In language, the pretraining objective was almost gifted to us—next token prediction just works, and the data was lying around on the internet. For vision and the physical world, we still haven't found an equivalently clean objective. People have tried contrastive learning, masked prediction, generative modeling, and each captures part of the picture. My own view is that generative models—diffusion, flow-based models—are going to play a bigger role here than people expect, not just as things that make nice images but as a way of learning world structure. If a model can predict what a scene looks like next, it has to understand something about physics and geometry, even if it never says a word about it.

The third thing, and this is more of a cultural point: I hope the field doesn't collapse into a single architecture and a single recipe. Transformers have been incredibly successful, and I've contributed to that in my own small way, but the moment where everyone is doing the same thing with more compute is usually the moment right before someone shows there's a better idea. I think there's still room for real architectural and representational research, especially for people in academia who can't match the compute but can ask different questions.

So if I had to summarize: I think LLMs are a stunning achievement, but I think they're a stepping stone. The system we actually want learns from the world the way we do—by looking, by predicting, by interacting—and language is one modality in that, not the foundation. The next few years will be about figuring out how to build that, and I don't think the answer is just a bigger language model with a camera attached.

r001.rationale: The response calls LLMs a stepping stone but does not say they will never disappear entirely.

r002.rationale: Calling LLMs a stepping stone and describing language as one modality rather than the foundation communicates a shift away from their prominence.

astra-6.text:
I think one important question is whether language alone is enough. Language is a powerful way to represent knowledge, but we also understand the world through what we see and how we interact with it. So I expect these models to become more closely connected to vision and action.

That opens up a different kind of challenge. A model can describe a scene, but can it understand what will change if you move an object? Can it make a prediction, take an action, and learn from the result? Those capabilities seem important if we want systems that can help beyond a conversation.

I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t assume that making models bigger automatically solves everything. We still need to understand their limitations and measure whether they’re becoming more reliable, rather than simply more convincing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how models may develop, but does not predict that large language models will never disappear entirely.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict that large language models will eventually fade in prominence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big question is whether language alone is enough. Language is incredibly powerful, but we also understand the world through what we see and how we interact with it. So I’m interested in how these models can connect language with visual understanding and, eventually, action.

There’s also a difference between producing a convincing answer and having a reliable understanding of something. Making progress on that distinction—figuring out what models actually learn and where they fail—seems just as important as making them bigger.

I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t assume we already know the path. We need to keep testing our assumptions and leave room for ideas beyond the current approach.

r001.rationale: The response does not predict that large language models will remain permanently; it says the future path is uncertain.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict that large language models will fade in prominence; it discusses connecting them with vision and action.
